column2: The robot's body
The body is the part that touches the real world: wheels, head and sensors. Do the work with the robot lifted, until Stage 8 passes.
What the body does

The robot's body is controlled by an ESP32 DevKit V1 on the 30P expansion board. It drives the wheels and head, reads all the sensors, and runs its own safety rules. The brain (ESP32-S3) only sends short commands such as M 150 150 800 (forward for 0.8 seconds).

Build the body
Stages 3 and 4 need the 6 V rail from Part 1. When USB is plugged into the DevKit, the 5 V wire from the LM2596 to the 30P board is unplugged (table mode).
Set up the DevKit on the 30P board
1 Power block: the left column is all GND, the right column holds the 5V and 3V pins (check in step 3). In run mode, 5 V from the LM2596 goes into one of these 5V pins.
2 V-pin voltage selector jumper: move it to the 3.3V–V position. All the V pins on the board then carry 3.3 V.
3 and 4: the pin rows for each GPIO (S = outermost signal, V, G). The row name is printed beside it: D25, D26, D23, D22, and so on.
5 I2C header: D22, D21, VCC, GND. Used by the MPU6050 in Stage 6.
6 DC jack 6.5-16 V: not used. 7 The board's USB port: power only, not used. Upload through the micro-USB port on the DevKit module.
The blink code runs on the DevKit, and you know which pins in the power block are 5 V and which are 3.3 V.
OK to lock in The 3.3V–V jumper position and the notes on the 5V and 3V pins in the power block. The DevKit stays on the 30P board: the two go up to level 2 as one unit.
Not yet The 30P board is not bolted down yet. On the robot it uses 8 mm nylon standoffs on level 2 (Part 6 Stage 3).
Port does not show up: your USB cable may be charge-only. Try another cable. The USB chip on the DevKit V1 is usually a CP2102: install the CP210x driver if needed.
Assemble the chassis and prepare the motors
The bottom plate with four TT motors and wheels.
Pair the 100 nF capacitor on each motor: across the two metal legs, one capacitor leg on each motor leg.

Seen from above, the positions match the robot exactly (see the layout drawing in Part 6). The numbers in the drawing = the numbers in the table and in the steps. Grey wires = motor wires (25, 26) and signal jumper wires (30-32).

Why this way? TT motors are designed for 3-6 V. Two motors on one side always move together (the robot turns by spinning the left and right sides in different directions), so one driver channel per side is enough.
Four motors firmly attached, and two pairs of wires: one for the left side, one for the right side.

OK to lock in The motors and wheels are mounted on the bottom plate, the 100 nF capacitors are soldered, the left and right wires are joined, and the heat shrink is closed. This part does not change again until the robot is finished.
Not yet The top plate is not mounted yet (Part 6 Stage 3). The female jumper ends on the motor wires stay plugged into the TB6612; no soldering needed.
TB6612FNG and motor test
The underside of your TB6612: pin names.
The top: the chip and the capacitor.
TB6612 power side (wires 17, 18) and motor wires (25, 26): the level-1 map in Stage 2.
Why this way? PWMA sets the speed (0-255) by switching on and off very fast (20,000 times per second). AIN1 and AIN2 set the direction: one HIGH and one LOW = turning, both the same = stopped.
The Serial Monitor prints LEFT forward, LEFT backward, RIGHT forward, RIGHT backward, and the matching wheels turn that way. "Forward" = the wheels turn as if the robot were walking forward.
OK to lock in The green and black wires from WAGO 6V and WAGO −6 to VM and GND of the TB6612 (female jumper soldered, heat shrink closed) and the 470 µF capacitor across WAGO 6V and WAGO −6.
Not yet The TB6612 is not strapped to the plate yet (cable ties, Part 6 Stage 2). The nine F-F signal wires to the 30P board are still table wires.
One side spins the wrong way: swap the two motor wires of that side at AO1/AO2 (or BO1/BO2). Or later change MOTOR_KIRI_TERBALIK in the body code.
One wheel on the same side spins opposite to the other: swap only the red-black of that motor.
No wheel turns: STBY is not at 3V, VM is not getting 6 V, or the DevKit GND is not connected to the TB6612 GND.
Wheels hum but do not turn: speed 150 is too low for your motors, or the XL4015 is below 6 V.
The DevKit restarts when the motors start: motor noise. Fit the 100 nF capacitors on the motors and check the shared GND.
Pan-tilt head (MG90S servos)
Your assembled pan-tilt. The bottom servo = pan, the top servo = tilt.

Head power joints: the two servo reds joined into one to the green, the two browns joined into one to the black, the 470 µF capacitor across the two joints (long leg + to the red side). The orange wires are not cut and each servo plug stays a single 3-hole block.
Why this way? A servo reads the pulse width 50 times per second: 0.6 ms = 0°, 1.5 ms = 90°, 2.4 ms = 180°. The tilt angle is limited to 40-150° in the code so the head does not hit the bracket.
The head looks left, center, right, then nods. Type 90 90 in the Serial Monitor: the head faces straight ahead.
OK to lock in The red-green and brown-black solder joints, and the 470 µF capacitor with heat shrink closed. The servo arm screws once the servo is still at 90°.

Not yet The head is not bolted to the third plate yet (Part 6 Stage 4). The TILT_MIN and TILT_MAX limits are only final once the head is mounted on the robot, because they depend on the bracket and the head position. The orange wires to D23 and D4 are still table wires.
A servo moves randomly, one servo stays still, or moves by itself when you touch the power wire: the servo GND is not connected to the DevKit GND. Repeat the beep test in the shared GND step.
A servo vibrates or hums constantly: not enough power. Make sure red goes to 6 V (not 3.3 V) and the capacitor is fitted.
A servo vibrates only at the end of its travel: the arm hits the bracket. Reduce the angle limit in the code and do not let the servo hold at the end.
The head hits the bracket at a certain angle: note the angle, then change TILT_MIN and TILT_MAX in the body code later.
Two HC-SR04 distance sensors
Two HC-SR04: one for the front, one for the rear.
Newly added parts appear bright, parts from earlier stages are faded. White dots = leg or wire ends in the holes. Tags on the top/bottom edge = wires going out to a board or sensor.

Why this way? The sensor sends an ultrasonic pulse, then the ECHO pin stays high for the round trip of the sound. Sound travels about 1 cm per 29 µs, round trip 58 µs per cm. The two sensors are read in turns so that the echo of one is not read by the other.

The front and rear numbers change as your hand gets closer. Try a wall: the number comes close to the distance measured with a ruler (a 1-2 cm difference is normal). -1 means no echo (too far, or the sensor is not connected).
OK to lock in The 1 kΩ and 2 kΩ divider resistors on breadboard 1. This breadboard goes up to level 2 together with the wires already plugged in (Part 6 Stage 3).
Not yet Do not lock in the two sensors: the rear one moves to level 1 and its wiring is rearranged (TRIG through the breadboard), and the front one is mounted at the front edge of level 2.
Always -1: VCC is not getting 5 V (check a30), or TRIG/ECHO are swapped.
Numbers jump around: slanted or soft surfaces (cloth, sofa) reflect sound badly. That is a property of this sensor.
Always 0 or a small fixed number: the 2 kΩ resistor is not connected to the blue line.
MPU6050 (tilt sensor)
MPU6050 (GY-521). The pin names are printed beside the holes.
Optional: weather sensor (BME280 or DHT11)
Skip this part if you do not use a weather sensor. The robot still runs without one; the temperature and humidity values are just empty.
Have a BME280: VIN → V pin of row D21, GND → G of row D21, SDA → S of row D21, SCL → S of row D22. One I2C bus can serve many sensors as long as their addresses differ.

Or the DHT11 from the weather station kit on the breadboard. The DHT11 legs (the perforated side facing you) go to f10–f13. Wire j10 → lower red rail, j13 → lower blue rail, 10 kΩ resistor from j11 to the lower red rail, wire h11 → S of row D5.
Test with the code below: besides the MPU6050, it reads the BME280 (address 0x76 or 0x77) or the DHT11 on GPIO 5.
BME280 not read even though the address is there: your module may be a BMP280 (no humidity). "nan" for the DHT11: check the leg order and the 10 kΩ resistor.

Why this way? The MPU6050 measures acceleration, including gravity. From the direction of gravity, the code works out how tilted the robot is. The body uses this to stop if the robot is upside down or lifted at a tilt.
The scan finds 0x68. When flat, pitch and roll are near 0 and the z acceleration is about 1 g; when tilted, the numbers change too. The gyro is near 0 when still and jumps when rotated.
OK to lock in The soldered MPU6050 header pins.

Not yet The MPU6050 is not stuck down yet. On the robot it must lie flat on level 1 with a 6 mm standoff, the writing facing forward (Part 6 Stage 2). If it is tilted, pitch and roll do not start from zero.
No address found: SDA and SCL are swapped, VCC or GND is not connected, or an F-F wire is loose.
Found 0x69, not 0x68: the AD0 pin is connected to VCC. Leave AD0 unconnected.
WHO_AM_I is not 0x68 (for example 0x70 or 0x98): a clone module. As long as pitch and roll make sense, it is still usable.
Numbers stuck at the same value or all 0: the module has not woken up or is broken. Unplug and replug the USB, check the header pin solder joints.
Battery gauge and STOP button

Why this way? GPIO 39 is input only and has no pull-up resistor inside the chip, so we add 10 kΩ to 3.3 V. Not pressed, the pin reads HIGH; pressed, the pin connects to GND and reads LOW. For the finished robot, the 6 mm button is replaced by a 12 mm button on the middle-left wing of level 3, connected with two wires to columns 27 and 29 (lengths in Part 6).
The battery voltage in the Serial Monitor matches the multimeter (difference under 0.1 V after calibration), and the text changes to DITEKAN when the button is pressed.
OK to lock in The 26 AWG battery-gauge wire (blue heat shrink) from LM2596 #1 IN+ to a20, and the 20 kΩ and 10 kΩ divider resistors. The BATERAI_FAKTOR value you calculated.

Not yet The 6 mm button is only for testing: in Part 6 Stage 3 it is removed and replaced by the 12 mm STOP button on level 3. The table GND wire (WAGO − to the G pin) is also only for testing: on the robot the shared GND comes from the LM2596 #1 black wire to the 30P board.
Battery reads 0: the BAT+ wire is not in a20, or the switch is OFF.
Battery reads 0 even though the multimeter at the WAGO reads 8 V, and a20 to the breadboard GND is also 0 V: the battery GND is not connected to the DevKit GND (shared GND step).

The battery number jumps to about 3100 mV or 140 mV by itself, and the button switches between DITEKAN/released untouched: the breadboard's top rail is not getting 3.3 V (the 3V and G pin wires from Stage 5 are not fitted), so the button's pull-up does not work and the input floats.
Button always DITEKAN: the button legs used are not diagonal. Rotate the button 90 degrees.
Upload the body code and run the safety test
Full code: download robot_badan.ino.

Why this way? The D line holds the front distance, rear distance, battery, temperature, humidity, pitch, roll and flags. The brain reads the same line over UART every 250 ms. Every movement stops by itself when its time runs out (max 3 seconds), so if the brain hangs or the UART wire comes loose, the robot does not run away.
The body obeys commands and refuses dangerous movements. In the Serial Monitor a data line such as D 45 120 7.92 29.5 70 1 -2 0 appears every second.
OK to lock in The BATERAI_FAKTOR value and the motor direction choices in robot_badan.ino. This code is used as is on the robot. Uploading the code is required before Part 3.
Not yet JARAK_STOP_DEPAN, TILT_MIN and TILT_MAX are only tuned after the robot is finished (Part 6 Stage 8). The safety test may be postponed to Part 6, but do not let it be missed.
